knowledge_points.label: Napkin math: largest model that fits in memory
knowledge_points.statement: With AdamW in mixed precision the lecture counts 12 bytes per parameter (2 param + 2 grad + 4 + 4 optimizer state), so 8×80 GB H100s hold ~53B parameters before activations.

anchors.quote: bytes_per_parameter = 2 + 2 + (4 + 4)
Caveat: activations are not accounted for ... so this is an upper bound.
What's the largest model you can train on H100s using AdamW? ... the number of bytes per parameter, which is 2 plus 2 plus 4 plus 4 ... going to be about 53 billion

provenance.filtering_note: L81 counts 2 + 2 + (4 + 4) = 12 bytes/parameter: bf16 params and grads plus two fp32 Adam moments, with no fp32 master copy. The blog the professor cites later does count a master copy (16). The lecture's own number is 12 → 53B. Spoken evidence (video 3:27-3:54): the professor frames both motivating numbers as shape, not precision: 'the point is not to precisely calculate every single thing, but just get the rough shape of things'. He promises to explain 2+2+4+4 later; the lecture explains AdaGrad's 4 and Adam's 8 bytes (1:10:45) but never the AdamW-specific breakdown again.

misconceptions.belief: Model memory = parameters × 2 bytes.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Training also stores gradients and two optimizer moments; that is 6× the bf16 parameter footprint.

misconceptions.belief: Adam's state costs the same as the parameters.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Two fp32 moments are 8 bytes per parameter, four times a bf16 parameter.

predict.q: 8 H100s (80 GB each), AdamW with the lecture's accounting: bf16 params, bf16 grads, two fp32 moments, no master copy. Largest parameter count that fits, ignoring activations? (billions)
predict.why: Bytes per parameter = 2 + 2 + (4 + 4) = 12 (L81). 640e9 / 12 ≈ 53e9. The professor's own @inspect value is num_parameters ≈ 5.3e10. With an fp32 master copy it would be 16 bytes and ~40B.
predict.targets_misconception: Adam's state costs the same as the parameters.

transfer.q: Same 8 H100s (640 GB total), but you swap AdamW for SGD with momentum, which keeps a single fp32 momentum buffer per parameter. Using the lecture's accounting (bf16 params and grads, no separate fp32 master copy), what is the largest model in billions of parameters?
transfer.why: Bytes per parameter fall from 12 to 2 + 2 + 4 = 8 (bf16 params, bf16 grads, one fp32 momentum buffer), so 640e9 / 8 = 80e9. The numerator is unchanged; only the optimizer term of the divisor changed (L81-L82).

retrieval.q: Bytes per parameter for AdamW training in bf16 with fp32 moments, per the lecture?
retrieval.answer: 12 = 2 (param) + 2 (grad) + 4 + 4 (two moments)

retrieval.q: The professor calls the ~53B figure an upper bound. Which memory cost is left out of the 12 bytes/parameter, and what two run settings does it depend on?
retrieval.answer: Activations; they depend on batch size and sequence length (L83).

prompts.self_explain: Which of the four terms would change if you trained in fp32 throughout?

steps.why: Every one of these lives for the whole step; the moments are fp32 because they accumulate small updates (the mixed-precision rule), so the optimizer state alone is 8 of the 12 bytes.

knowledge_points.label: Floating point formats and bytes per element
knowledge_points.statement: fp32 = 4 bytes; fp16 and bf16 = 2 bytes; bf16 keeps fp32's exponent range but has coarser mantissa; fp8 (E4M3/E5M2) = 1 byte.

anchors.quote: bf16 uses the same memory as fp16 but has the same dynamic range as fp32!
x = torch.tensor([1e-8], dtype=torch.float16) ... assert x == 0  # Underflow!
H100s support two variants of FP8: E4M3 (range [-448, 448]) and E5M2
One of the bits is a sign, 8 bits are the exponent, which gives you dynamic range
if you train with fp16, which people did back in the day, you will get instability ... You will get underflow ... You'll get NaNs
because things are kind of sloppy and stochastic anyway, you don't need that much resolution

provenance.filtering_note: Professor shows the underflow live (1e-8 in fp16 becomes 0, in bf16 does not) rather than deriving exponent widths. Wikipedia figures are shown, not explained. Spoken evidence (video 10:30-10:54): the reason bf16's coarse mantissa is acceptable is given only aloud: training is 'sloppy and stochastic anyway', so range matters more than resolution; fp16 training failure modes are named as underflow, overflow and NaNs (9:35-9:49). Correction to the note above: the audio shows the fp16 1e-8 underflow (9:10) but then 'let me actually skip over this part' (10:54) right after the bf16 explanation, so the bf16 no-underflow demo (L148-L149) was most likely skipped in class, not shown live. fp8 variants are explicitly not covered (13:37).

misconceptions.belief: bf16 is just a less precise fp16.
misconceptions.why_wrong: bf16 trades mantissa bits for exponent bits: same range as fp32, worse resolution. fp16 has the opposite trade.

predict.why: fp16's smallest subnormal is ~6e-8; bf16 shares fp32's 8-bit exponent and represents 1e-8 fine.

check.varies: the inverse direction: bytes are given and the parameter count is asked

retrieval.q: Which has larger dynamic range, fp16 or bf16, and what did that cost?

prompts.self_explain: Why does giving bf16 more exponent bits fix the 1e-8 underflow without making it more precise than fp16?

steps.do: fp16 has a 5-bit exponent: its smallest positive value is the subnormal 2⁻²⁴ ≈ 5.96e-8.
steps.why: Below that, fp16 has no representable number except 0.

steps.do: 1e-8 is less than half of 2⁻²⁴ (≈ 2.98e-8), so it rounds to 0: the assert x == 0 at L142 holds.
steps.why: Rounding goes to the nearest representable value, and 0 is nearer than 5.96e-8. That is the underflow the code calls a source of instability.

steps.do: bf16 keeps fp32's 8-bit exponent (smallest normal 2⁻¹²⁶ ≈ 1.2e-38) with only 7 mantissa bits, so 1e-8 is stored as about 1.0012e-8, not 0.
steps.why: Range comes from exponent bits, resolution from mantissa bits: bf16 spends its 16 bits on range ('same dynamic range as fp32') and pays in resolution.

presentations.notice: why losing mantissa bits is an acceptable trade in deep learning

knowledge_points.label: Mixed precision training
knowledge_points.statement: Use bf16 for parameters, activations and gradients; keep optimizer state in fp32 for stability.

anchors.quote: Use bf16 for parameters, activations, and gradients; Use fp32 for optimizer states
if you're training a small model ... just float32 is fine ... So bf16 is the sweet spot.
bf16 is what you would use for parameters, activations, and gradients ... And for optimizer states, you would use fp32.
it's customary to use fp32 for the optimizer states for stability reasons ... you're taking squares, and you're averaging multiple steps

provenance.filtering_note: The 2017 paper's key device, fp32 master weights plus loss scaling, is not mentioned. Professor keeps the rule and drops the mechanism. Spoken evidence: (1) advice absent from the code: for a small model 'just float32 is fine' (11:05-11:15); (2) the reason optimizer state stays fp32, stated at 1:10:24-1:10:45: people have tried bf16, but the state squares gradients and averages over many steps, which is not stable at low precision; (3) AMP is introduced with 'We're not going to talk too much about this' (12:40), so the autocast policy beyond 'matmuls safe, exp not' is filtered out.

predict.why: Accumulating averages over many steps needs resolution, which bf16 lacks (L641).

transfer.q: You observe the loss going NaN when training in pure fp16 but not bf16. Which property of fp16 is the likely cause?

check.q: An activation with value 70,000 is cast to fp16 and to bf16. Which casts produce inf?
distractor_from: 'bf16 only' <- misconception (neighbouring KP dtype-bytes): 'bf16 is just a less precise fp16.' (assumes bf16 is worse on every axis)

knowledge_points.label: einsum as named contraction
knowledge_points.statement: einsum names each axis; axes that appear in inputs but not the output are summed over. It replaces transposes and reshapes with a readable spec.

anchors.quote: z = einsum(x, y, "seq1 hidden, hidden seq2 -> seq1 seq2")
y = reduce(x, "... hidden -> ...", "sum") ... x = rearrange(x, "... (heads hidden1) -> ... heads hidden1", heads=2)
the way to think about einsum is a generalized matrix multiplication with good bookkeeping
anything that is not mentioned here, the hidden gets summed out
Is there some speed-up to this? ... You can think about it as just sugar.

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken evidence (video 23:50-23:57): asked whether einops is faster, the professor says it reduces to the same primitive operations, 'just sugar'; the benefit is readability (no transposes to reason about). He covers only the basics and points to the tutorial (19:10), and says rearrange 'will come up in an assignment once' (24:10).

misconceptions.why_wrong: Any axis omitted from the output is reduced; batch axes are kept only because they are written on the right.

knowledge_points.label: FLOPs of a matrix multiply
knowledge_points.statement: A (B×D)·(D×K) matmul costs 2·B·D·K FLOPs: one multiply and one add per (i, j, k) triple.

anchors.quote: actual_num_flops = 2 * B * D * K
FLOPs: floating-point operations (measure of computation done) ... FLOP/s: floating-point operations per second
this is going to be 2 times basically the product of all the three dimensions ... we have one multiplication for each triple and then also one addition
I think the way the hardware is built, the two are basically the same
the number of FLOPs in order to do a forward pass of this linear matrix is actually 2 times the number of tokens or data points times the number of parameters

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken evidence (video 33:59-34:45): the bridge from 2·B·D·K to '2 × tokens × parameters' (the seed of 6ND) is made aloud here, while the code states it only later in gradients_flops. Also spoken: the −1 in D−1 additions is dropped on purpose (32:11-32:22); adds and multiplies cost the same on the hardware (33:42); sub-cubic matmul algorithms are set aside because practical gains come from co-design with the systems, not asymptotics (33:10-33:32).

misconceptions.belief: A matmul costs B·D·K.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Each of the B·D·K products is also accumulated, so multiply by 2.

knowledge_points.label: Elementwise FLOPs are negligible next to matmul FLOPs
knowledge_points.statement: An elementwise op on an m×n tensor costs about c·mn FLOPs (c a small per-element constant), while the matmul that produced it costs 2·m·n·k, so for a large inner dimension k the FLOP count is dominated by matmuls; this says nothing about time, because elementwise ops are memory-bound.

anchors.quote: elementwise operations are just the size of a matrix ... addition also requires m n FLOPs ... no other operation you'll encounter as expensive as matrix multiplication for large enough matrices ... with important caveat of when we talk about memory

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only (video 32:31-32:58). The code goes straight from 'what is a FLOP' to the linear model's 2·B·D·K and never says why counting only matmuls is safe. The professor gives the rule and its limit in one breath: 'for large enough matrices', 'with important caveat of when we talk about memory'. The caveat is cashed out later by the GELU intensity example (L400-L415). The 20 FLOPs/element for GELU used in the prompts is the lecture's own estimate (L406).

misconceptions.belief: GELU's ~20 FLOPs per element make it a significant share of a layer's compute.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Per output element the matmul does 2k FLOPs (k = inner dimension, thousands), so 20 is a fraction of a percent once k is large.

misconceptions.belief: A tiny FLOP share means a tiny share of wall-clock time.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Elementwise ops are memory-bound (intensity ~5 vs ~295 for an H100); their time is set by bytes moved, not FLOPs.

predict.q: A layer computes h = x·W with x of shape 4096×4096 (batch × D) and W of shape 4096×4096, then applies GELU (about 20 FLOPs per element, the lecture's estimate) to h. What fraction of the layer's total FLOPs is the GELU? Give a decimal.
predict.why: GELU: 20·B·D. Matmul: 2·B·D·D. Share = 20 / (20 + 2·4096) ≈ 0.0024, about a quarter of a percent.
predict.targets_misconception: GELU's ~20 FLOPs per element make it a significant share of a layer's compute.

transfer.q: Same layer and the same batch of 4096, but the hidden size D is only 64 (W is 64×64). What fraction of the layer's FLOPs is the GELU now? Give a decimal.
transfer.why: Share = 20 / (20 + 2·64) = 20/148 ≈ 0.135. The rule holds 'for large enough matrices': with a small inner dimension, elementwise FLOPs stop being negligible.
transfer.invariant: elementwise cost c·B·D vs matmul cost 2·B·D·D

check.q: Hold the batch fixed and double the hidden size D of a D×D linear layer followed by GELU. Does GELU's share of the layer's FLOPs go up, go down, or stay the same?
check.answer: down (roughly halves, since the share is about 10/D)
check.why: Elementwise FLOPs grow like B·D, matmul FLOPs like B·D², so the elementwise share falls like 1/D.

retrieval.q: Write the FLOP counts of an elementwise op on an m×n matrix and of the matmul (m×k)(k×n) that produced it.
retrieval.answer: About c·mn for the elementwise op (c FLOPs per element) vs 2·m·n·k for the matmul.

retrieval.q: GELU is 0.24% of a 4096-wide layer's FLOPs. Why can't you conclude it takes 0.24% of the layer's time?
retrieval.answer: It is memory-bound: its arithmetic intensity (~5 FLOPs/byte) is far below the accelerator's (~295), so its time is set by reading and writing the tensor, not by its FLOPs.

knowledge_points.label: Timing GPU code needs synchronize
knowledge_points.statement: GPU kernels launch asynchronously, so a timer must call torch.cuda.synchronize() before starting and after the operation; without it you time only the launch and the measured FLOP/s comes out impossibly high. Time several runs and average.

anchors.quote: you have to call cuda synchronize to make sure that-- because the GPU is running asynchronously ... If you omit this, you're going to find that wow, your timings are really fast. ... And that's because this is a non-blocking call.
it's general good practice to try this multiple times and take the average

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only. The lecture's benchmark() helper (lecture_02.py L830-L848) calls torch.cuda.synchronize() twice with bare comments ('Wait until CUDA threads are done'), but the text never says what goes wrong without it. The failure mode ('wow, your timings are really fast', 'a non-blocking call') exists only in the audio. Benchmarking proper is deferred to a later lecture ('in the few lectures, we're going to talk more about benchmarking', 35:18). The numbers in the prompts are the author's.

prerequisites.note: Measured FLOP/s = counted FLOPs ÷ measured time.

misconceptions.belief: Wrapping `y = x @ w` in time.time() calls measures the matmul.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The call only enqueues a kernel and returns; the GPU is still working when the second timestamp is taken.

misconceptions.belief: A benchmark showing more FLOP/s than the datasheet means the GPU is faster than advertised.
misconceptions.why_wrong: You never get more than promised (MFU ≤ 1); an above-peak number means the timer stopped before the work finished.

predict.q: You time y = x @ w on an H100 (about 1.1e12 FLOPs) with time.time() before and after the line, without synchronize, and get 20 µs. What does that 20 µs mostly measure?
choices: The matmul itself, which simply ran very fast
Launching the kernel: the call returned before the GPU finished
Copying x and w from CPU memory to the GPU
Python interpreter overhead of evaluating the @ operator
predict.answer: Launching the kernel: the call returned before the GPU finished

retrieval.q: With checkpoints every √L layers, which two sets of activations are alive at the memory peak during backward?

presentations.notice: During backward only one segment is refilled at a time, from its own checkpoint: the resident bar peaks at checkpoints + one segment (4 + 4 = 8 of 16) and then falls.
Peak memory L/k + k is U-shaped in k with its minimum at k = √L, while recomputation stays one forward pass; 'store nothing' drops memory to a constant but makes recomputation grow like L².

steps.do: Store every layer: L activations resident during backward, nothing recomputed: O(L) memory.
steps.why: This is the default the other options are measured against (L771).

steps.do: Checkpoint every k layers: L/k checkpoints stay resident, and backward through one segment recomputes its k layers from the segment's checkpoint.
steps.why: Only one segment is refilled at a time, so at the peak you hold all checkpoints plus one segment.

steps.do: The sum is smallest at k = √L. For L = 64, k = 8: 8 checkpoints + 8 recomputed layers = 16 = 2√L, so memory is O(√L).
steps.why: L/k shrinks and k grows as the segments lengthen; they balance where L/k = k.

steps.do: Recomputation: every layer is recomputed once, from its own segment's checkpoint, about L layer-forwards in total: O(L), one extra forward pass.
steps.why: Each segment starts from a stored checkpoint, so no layer has to be rebuilt from the network input.

presentations.notice: checkpointing each linear+ReLU block halves activation memory by not storing the pre-ReLU tensor
